en: Ferraz Jr. formulates the point in terms that serve as a rule of method: “absorption of insecurity” means that the act of deciding “transforms undecidable incompatibilities into decidable alternatives”, without promising to eliminate the conflict, but converting it into something tractable <1>Jr.</1><2>(Ferraz Jr., 2003, [p. 312])</2>. In platform-governed consumption, this implies that control must not be confused with the ambition of seeing everything. It must be understood as the construction of verifiable requirements that make modulation legally decidable.

In this fit, Ávila's distinction between security and transparency provides an additional protection against deviations. Ávila records that transparency has its “conceptual core linked to the idea of information”, while security centers on the “rational-argumentative question”, aiming to “ensure rationality and effectiveness to Law as a whole” and not merely to “inform” <1>Ávila</1><2>(Ávila, 2011, p. 255-256)</2>. Technical opacity, by itself, does not function as a free zone of liability. It shifts the axis of control to public, contestable and auditable criteria applicable to decisions that modulate enjoyment. Open auditability defines the minimum of verifiability necessary to reconstruct what was done and why. Functional value equivalence defines the material parameter for judging whether utility was preserved or whether there was a substantial downgrade disguised as an update.

<1>p. 482</1> With this, the two operators stabilize as criteria of legitimacy and of restoration in continuous digital services. Open auditability prevents governance by architecture from operating as a power immune to verification, especially when sanctions and reconfigurations substantially affect positions of enjoyment without total interruption. Functional value equivalence prevents the inherent mutability of continuous supply from being converted into an instrument of unilateral downgrading of content and quality, including in socially verifiable symbolic dimensions, treated as cultural correlations and not as mental states. Together, the operators make controllable, under opacity and mutability, the distinction between legitimate adaptation oriented to maintaining utility and emptying reconfiguration that requires a legal response compatible with the CDC and its regime for the IOC.

The updates clause of the Terms of Service makes explicit that supply is conceived as evolutionary and that changes may affect even virtual products, with a unilateral power of modification and automatic updating. Furthermore, it provides that the company may “use background patches” to automatically update games and <1>software</1> “with or without prior notice” <2>Riot Games</2><3>(Riot Games, 2024e)</3>. In addition, the limitation of liability includes the idea that the company is not responsible for damages if the user did not install updates when made available, or did not maintain minimum specifications, by stating that “we are also not responsible for any damage that occurs because you did not install any update when it is made available” <4>Riot Games</4><5>(Riot Games, 2024e)</5>. The legally relevant effect is to recognize that the contractual regime itself is responsible for normalizes continuous modulation, automated updating and the shifting of compatibility costs and risks. If this is an assumed pattern, protection does not depend on denying updates, but on demanding controllable criteria for comparison and, when there is a relevant impact on utility, a path of restoration that prevents the consumer from being trapped in a substantial substitution imposed through opacity. <6>↩</6>

In a public text dedicated to the subject, the company describes the visual effects update program as an improvement aimed at consistency, readability and graphic quality, describing that the updates are made to “improve overall gameplay consistency, readability and graphic quality” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2022a)</2>. In making its criteria explicit, the text includes ranked objectives and a hierarchy of importance, maintaining that one of the objectives is to “reduce overall visual noise”, for example by “reducing the ‘invasion’ of textures that have many fine and unnecessary details”, and also states that the objectives are “ranked in order of importance”, so that “the readability of gameplay mechanics will always prevail over thematic resonance” <3>Riot Games</3><4>(Riot Games, 2022a)</4>. This kind of statement is valuable because it reveals an institutional pattern of decision, not an isolated event. The point is not to contest the legitimacy of the pursuit of clarity, but to recognize that the application of these criteria may, in specific cases, reconfigure the core of utility that motivated the purchase of a cosmetic, especially when part of the value is tied to the visual experience, to distinction and to the perceived “weight” in game. <5>↩</5>

The official “Patch Notes” channel functions as the recurring public record of changes to the game, organized in periodic entries, by patch, with titles and dates <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, [202-?]b)</2>. The format is useful for general information and for minimal communicative transparency, but it is not designed as a tool of comparative auditability aimed at the consumer who needs to technically reconstruct a before and after of a specific cosmetic, with objective parameters of demonstration. The consequence, for dogmatics is simple. In a regime in which the supplier can update continuously and even automatically, auditability cannot depend on the chance that the consumer has archived evidence or has the technical knowledge to produce handmade comparisons. If the system does not deliver, as a standard, sufficient comparative elements, the control of functional downgrading requires either clearer public criteria for change or restoration mechanisms as automated as that dispense with impossible proof when the impact is relevant. <3>↩</3>

Having set the general frame of the IOC regime, the next step is to present its structuring categories in a dogmatic key, so as to make manageable what has so far been stated as apparatus. The central question, at this point, is not to repeat the map of the regime, but to show how the categories connect to one another and why this connection is what sustains the legal controllability of continuous platform-governed consumption. Without this internal articulation, each category could be read in isolation, as a conceptual label for a specific problem, and would lose the capacity to operate as a unified language for abuses by design, relevant degradations and proportional responses.

The starting point is not the object, but the position of the consumer that this object meets. Semiotic vulnerability names, in a legal key, the structural inequality of intelligibility and agency that defines this position in environments in which value, belonging and recognition are mediated by signs, visibility regimes and internal metrics administered by the supplier itself. Presenting it first is not expository arbitrariness, but recognition that it functions as a key for reading what follows. Without understanding that the consumer inhabits an environment whose intelligibility is partially reserved to the supplier, the definition of the Immaterial Object of Consumption as a enjoyment bundle sustained over time would appear as a mere technical description of the digital good, and not as a category that organizes attribution, proof and restoration under the Consumer Protection Code.

Having identified the position of the consumer and the object that this position sees, there follows the description of the unlawful act that may operate between the two. Abusive teleology occupies this place as an unlawful act of architecture, that is, as a mode of attribution that reaches exploitative purposes inscribed in the technical-organizational design of the service, and not only in textual contractual commands. Its formulation depends on the two previous categories. There is no legally capturable abusive teleology <1>p. 395</1> without the structural asymmetry that it exploits, nor without the enjoyment bundle that it degrades, which is why the test of five cumulative requirements, developed in its own subsection, only becomes applicable when semiotic vulnerability and the IOC have already been dogmatically fixed.

Next, personal integrity comes in to name the legal interests whose erosion constitutes the relevant injury. It is a category with two faces that operate in articulation, and not as separate categories. The functional face protects the performance, use and utility actually delivered. The identity and symbolic face protects belonging, reputation, distinction and the promise of recognition mediated by signs of the environment. The two faces must be thought of together because the enjoyment of the IOC is not realized by separating one from the other, and because the relevant degradation of continuous consumption usually falls simultaneously on both, as happens when a unilateral reconfiguration preserves technical access but downgrades the reputational or symbolic position of the consumer in the ecosystem.

Finally, open auditability and functional value equivalence close the regime as operational criteria without which the whole apparatus would remain merely declaratory. Open auditability requires minimum verifiability about what was promised, about what was changed and about the criteria of visibility, restriction and sanction, without confusing this requirement with total transparency or with indiscriminate disclosure of industrial secrets. Functional value equivalence provides the substantive yardstick to distinguish ordinary variation of digital dynamics from significant degradation of the enjoyment bundle, preventing every update from being treated as an unlawful act and every restoration from being reduced to economic restitution that ignores what was really contracted and lived.

The gearwork formed by these five categories is not a catalog of independent problems nor an inventory of topics related by affinity. It is a dogmatic articulation in which semiotic vulnerability describes the condition, the IOC describes the object, abusive teleology describes the unlawful act, personal integrity describes the protected legal interests and open auditability with functional value equivalence describe the operational criteria of verification and restoration.

The cut by digitally based business models requires delimiting, first of all, the type of ecosystem in which the immaterial object of consumption manifests itself most clearly. In environments sustained by continued enjoyment, the acquired utility is not realized as an isolated event, because it depends on a technical-organizational arrangement in permanent operation, in which infrastructure, interfaces, rules of use, validation mechanisms and sanction instruments integrate the very experience of enjoyment. In this configuration, the consumed object does not present itself as a detachable thing, but as a situation of enjoyment whose practical stability is conditioned by private governance and by ordinary modulations of the environment.

The framing has a strictly operative purpose. It seeks to fix minimum parameters to compare distinct objects and arrangements of supply in digital ecosystems, preventing the empirical analysis from degrading into a catalog of peculiarities and preventing the dogmatic reconstruction from resting on excessively general categories, incapable of discriminating relevant losses, asymmetries of agency and materially significant variations of utility and value. For this reason, the description that follows is deliberately oriented by recurring structures, with no claim to exhaustiveness nor attribution of generic intentions to platforms.

An IOC ecosystem can be described as a technical-organizational arrangement that sustains and conditions enjoyment over time, integrating continued operation, private governance and update cycles that define, in practical terms, what counts as admissible use, recognized performance, displayable collection and preserved or degraded position in the system. In these terms, the consumed object is not reduced to isolated content nor to an abstract promise of access. Its utility depends on conditions of enjoyment built and maintained by the ecosystem itself.

The first structural trait of this type of ecosystem is continued enjoyment. It shifts the focus from one-off delivery to the maintenance of the conditions of use over time. The acquired utility is realized through a sequence of acts of operation, updating, curation and enforcement of rules, so that continuity of the bond and minimum predictability of the conditions of enjoyment integrate the material content of supply. This structure alters the way of recognizing relevant losses: instead of depending on a single event of “access cut off”, the loss may occur through cumulative erosions of utility, functional downgrades and gradual shifts in the cost of remaining, even if access remains formally available.

The second decisive trait is the private governance of the environment of enjoyment. The platform does not merely enable access. It defines, operationally, the conditions of remaining and the <1>p. 486</1> forms of use of the object. Conduct policies, eligibility criteria, performance parameters, ranking mechanisms, visibility rules, validation procedures and sanction regimes make up a normative set incorporated into the architecture of the environment. This set does not regulate only externalities, since it determines, directly, how utility manifests itself, is maintained and can be restricted, and concentrates centers of practical decision that modulate enjoyment under structural asymmetries of information.

The third common trait is the constant modulation of access and value. In digital ecosystems, update cycles, interface reconfigurations, parameter adjustments and revisions of internal policies are an ordinary part of the functioning of the environment. Under these conditions, access is not expressed merely as a binary of availability. The way of enjoying depends on criteria that can be changed without the object formally ceasing to exist. Changes in rules of use, in eligibility criteria, in validation mechanisms and in visibility devices reorganize the content of enjoyment, defining what it is possible to do, display, accumulate or convert into utility within the system. Modulation, moreover, can reconfigure the value associated with the object, even when access remains intact, through changes in balancing, rarity, criteria for obtaining and reputational metrics.

The fourth trait is the structural dependence of the consumer on the ecosystem. Account, credentials, servers, use policies, validation mechanisms and internal visibility criteria constitute conditions of possibility of enjoyment and remain under the supplier's control. For this reason, the object is not fully appropriable outside the technical-organizational arrangement that sustains it. The intensity of this dependence varies according to the degree of lock-in, the centrality of collections tied to the account, the relevance of the usage history, the weight of reputation metrics and restrictions on transfer, interoperability or reconstruction of what was acquired outside the platform. These variables tend to operate cumulatively, causing the permanence of the bond and the practical acceptability of unilateral changes to become components of the material content of what was acquired.
These traits manifest themselves, with particular clarity, in three digital business models: games operated as a service, marketplaces and artificial intelligence services supplied by platform.

In games as a service, enjoyment is sustained by an environment in continuous operation in which the utility of the object depends on account, inventory, progression parameters, events, updates and rules of coexistence. What is acquired is composed of layers administered by the ecosystem, such as access to modes of enjoyment, content made available by season, items <1>p. 487</1> tied to the profile, permissions of use and criteria of permanence. The governance of the environment acts as a constitutive component of enjoyment. In this sense, parameter adjustments, store reconfigurations, revisions of internal policies and balance changes can reconfigure utility and the cost of remaining without formal interruption of access.

Furthermore, games as a service frequently incorporate an intense symbolic dimension, in which distinction, belonging and recognition are realized through visibility devices, reputation metrics, signs of rarity and forms of displaying the collection. For this reason, changes in rarity criteria, in display conditions, in rules of use and in validation mechanisms can produce relevant losses linked to symbolic identity, even when enjoyment remains formally available.

In digital marketplaces, the layer of mediation governed by the platform materially conditions the consumer's appropriation of value, even if the immediate object is material or immaterial. Curation, ranking, reputation, dispute policies, display criteria, delivery parameters and verification mechanisms structure the possibility of finding, comparing, contracting and validating what is acquired. It is not asserted, with this, that every digital mediation automatically converts any good into an IOC. The point is to recognize that, in certain arrangements, the layer of mediation functions as a continuous technical-organizational environment that integrates supply, because it conditions practical predictability, the intelligibility of the offer and the capacity to validate the result. Modulations in visibility algorithms, reputational metrics, recommendation patterns, return policies, anti-fraud rules and dispute parameters can reconfigure risks, transaction costs and the practical viability of choices without taking the form of explicit interruption. Structural dependence manifests itself through the concentration, in the platform, of transaction records, reputational credentials and decision-making instances, intensifying asymmetries of intelligibility and agency.

In artificial intelligence services supplied by platform, the consumed object is configured as a functional capacity made available under technical and normative parameters administered by the supplier. The utility of what is acquired depends on the continuous functioning of the system, its versions, its models and its use policies. Usage limits, authorization criteria, content filters, forms of performance prioritization and rules of interaction integrate the practical existence of the object, which is realized as an enjoyable capacity under variable conditions of governance. Modulation is constitutive, given that version changes, parameter adjustments, policy revisions, performance variations and reconfigurations of safeguards can alter results, restrict functionalities or reorganize costs of enjoyment without formal cancellation of access. Structural dependence becomes <1>p. 488</1> evident through the practical impossibility of replicating outside the ecosystem elements that condition the utility of the object, such as computational infrastructure, model updating and moderation criteria, reinforcing asymmetries of intelligibility and agency as to the reasons for and impacts of successive changes.

The approximation between these three models stems from a common structural core: in all of them, enjoyment depends on the continuous operation of a privately governed technical-organizational environment, in which rules, interfaces, metrics and validation procedures integrate the content of supply and remain susceptible to modulation over time. This convergence explains why relevant losses are not necessarily expressed as formal interruptions: modulation can downgrade use value, shift costs of remaining, alter conditions of visibility and reconfigure forms of validation without suppressing access, while structural dependence intensifies asymmetries of intelligibility and agency.

With the framing concluded, the next stage consists of converting the identified structural pattern into comparable classes oriented by criteria, capable of expressing how the object exists in the ecosystem and to what extent its enjoyment is sensitive to unilateral changes. This passage will allow preliminary categories of IOC on game platforms to be organized and the study of the legal regime applicable to the ecosystem studied to proceed, with discipline and controllability.

Once the ecosystem of continued enjoyment has been delimited, it becomes possible to organize a typology that stabilizes comparability between objects and arrangements of supply on game platforms. In these architectures, the acquired utility is realized over time and under private governance of the technical-organizational environment. The object of consumption, therefore, does not present itself as a detachable thing, but as a position of enjoyment conditioned by rules, interfaces, validation mechanisms and ordinary modulations.

So that the analysis does not degrade into a catalog of peculiarities and so that the dogmatic reconstruction does not operate with abbreviations that collapse heterogeneous arrangements, an instrument is needed that is capable of discriminating, consistently, what varies irrelevantly and what materially alters the enjoyment and value of what is acquired, including when the loss manifests itself through gradual degradation, functional downgrading or disorganization of symbolic value without formal interruption of access.

<1>p. 489</1> This typology is deliberately internal to the games laboratory and is not offered as a general classification of platforms. Its function is to allow that, within an ecosystem that concentrates hybrid objects and dense governance, the analysis recognizes patterns of mutability and of loss through verifiable equivalences, without depending on episodic descriptions. The transposition of the IOC regime to other families of platform will be developed in a specific stage of adherence tests, in which the already stabilized dogmatic parameters will be confronted with typical situations of continuous digital consumption in distinct ecosystems. Thus, it is established that the typology proposed below is internal and strictly operational to the model studied.

The first category is that of cosmetic-ornamental objects. These are IOCs whose utility is not exhausted in functional performance attributes, since it incorporates symbolic value realized as distinction, belonging and recognition in the ecosystem. Enjoyment depends on a tie to account, inventory and mechanisms of visibility and display that make what is acquired visible to third parties. Changes in display criteria, inventory organization, rules of admissible use, criteria for obtaining and rarity regimes can materially depreciate enjoyment even when the item remains available. In these cases, the relevant loss appears as disorganization of the sign-value incorporated into the object, and restoration is not exhausted in undifferentiated compensation, and must be assessed by functional value equivalence compatible with the symbolic nature of what is acquired.

The second category is that of progression objects. In it, the object is realized as a trajectory governed by rules, parameters and validation mechanisms administered by the ecosystem. What is acquired is not confused with a mere record of time invested, but with an enjoyable position built by goals, requirements and rewards defined by internal criteria. Unilateral modulation falls on parameters for obtaining, eligibility requirements, difficulty calibrations and criteria for recognizing performance. Successive changes can reorganize the relationship between effort and result, raise costs of remaining or make rewards impracticable, generating functional degradation without explicit cancellation. The requirement of controllability falls on the reconstruction of what changed and of which material effects were produced, in addition to the assessment of restorations according to the preservation of the bundle of utility incorporated into the trajectory.

The third category is that of access and permanence objects. These are IOCs marked by intense dependence on account, credentials and eligibility, so that enjoyment takes on, in practice, the form of a revocable position. The object is not reduced to the initial act of enabling, since it involves the maintenance of the conditions that make it possible to remain in the ecosystem and to use, on a continued basis, functionalities, modes of enjoyment and collections tied to the profile. <1>p. 490</1> Policy modulations and governance decisions, such as restrictions, suspensions and partial limitations, can degrade the consumer's position and radiate cascading effects on the collection and on the trajectory of enjoyment. In this category, open auditability assumes a central role, since the minimum required is verifiable justification and traceability of the measure, with an intelligible delimitation of what was decided and of its material effects, without imposing total technical transparency.

The fourth category is that of functionality objects. These are instrumental capacities made available to the consumer under technical and normative parameters administered by the supplier, such as permissions of use, convenience utilities, configuration possibilities and conversion capacities that integrate the bundle of utility of the ecosystem. Unilateral modulation manifests itself through reconfiguration of parameters, restrictions of use, interface changes and redistribution of capacities among modalities of enjoyment. Relevant losses appear as functional degradation of the bundle of utility, with increased operational friction, reduced capacity and downgrading of conveniences incorporated into what is acquired, even if access remains intact. Adequate restoration must be assessed by functional value equivalence, considering the capacity actually enjoyed and the materiality of the change.

The fifth category is that of time objects. It covers temporal structures that condition when, for how long and under which windows enjoyment can occur, such as validity regimes, seasons, availability cycles and frequency limits. In this class, time integrates the material content of supply. Changes of windows, redefinition of deadlines, reorganization of cycles and recalibration of limits can reconfigure utility, the cost of remaining and the practical viability of enjoying what is acquired without suppressing access. Relevant losses take the form of loss of opportunity and material downgrading of the temporal investment, especially when changes shift the balance between effort, reward and permanence.

The sixth category is that of reputation objects. They correspond to positions of recognition instituted by the ecosystem through metrics, validation criteria and visibility devices. Reputation is not reduced to stored data, since it depends on calculation rules, display criteria and validation systems that make it socially intelligible and comparable. Modulations of ranking criteria, display changes, governance decisions and sanctioning measures can reorganize the reputational position without interruption of access. Relevant losses manifest themselves as symbolic harm and disorganization of the place of recognition, with repercussions on the very utility of the environment. For this reason, the requirement of auditability is particularly sensitive, and changes and decisions that affect reputation <1>p. 491</1> must offer a verifiable minimum of justification and traceability, while restorations must be assessed by functional equivalence compatible with the reputational nature of the object.

The immediate application of this grid to concrete objects of the laboratory shows how typological categories can correspond to distinct modes of supply and conditioning, without reducing the ecosystem to an inventory of items. A first example, typical of a progression object, is the event pass, in which the acquisition is not directed at a ready result, but at access to a metered trajectory of milestones and rewards that is realized through tasks, game routines and internal validations. The mechanics are structured so that progress occurs over the course of the event and so that a relevant part of the rewards depends on the purchase of the pass, so that the consumer does not buy only “content”, but a form of active permanence to make enjoyable what was made available as potentiality <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024b)</2><3><4>471</4></3>.

This design is compatible with the very contractual frame of access to virtual content, in which the supplier recognizes that the license may be obtained not only by purchase, but also by earning, including through “game missions or tasks”, which makes it methodologically controllable to describe the pass as a progression object in the strict sense, that is, as an acquired and governed trajectory, and not as simple one-off consumption <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>.

As an example of a time object, the platform mobilizes regimes of availability and return to produce windows, cycles and rarities that integrate the material content of enjoyment. In operational language accessible to the public, certain categories of <1>skins</1> are treated as “legacy” or “limited”, with variations on whether or not they return to the store and under which conditions, so that the symbolic utility of what is acquired comes to depend, also, on an institutionally administered temporality <2>Riot Games</2><3>(Riot Games, 2025h)</3><4><5>472</5></4>.

<1>p. 492</1> In this case, the contractual frame that grants the supplier the power to exclude, alter, move, remove and reprice virtual content at any time, with or without notice, provides the minimum declaratory axis for reading the administration of availability as an ordinary variable of supply, which shifts the legal problem to the assessment of relevant losses through opportunity, through recalibration of windows and through reconfiguration of rarity, without confusing formal continuity of access with material preservation of the value enjoyed <2>Riot Games</2><3>(Riot Games, 2024e)</3>.

Finally, an example of a reputation object can be seen in the way the ecosystem conditions utilities and loot on metrics of conduct and eligibility. The honor system operates as a mechanism of comparable and socially intelligible recognition, but, at the same time, as everyday discipline, since behavior penalties can lock reputational progression and affect, in practice, access to rewards associated with the creation of loot, such as keys and capsules <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2017a)</2>.

Reputation, thus, does not appear as an extra-legal ornament of consumption, but as a condition of enjoyment administered by rules of conduct and by sanctioning decisions with cascading patrimonial and symbolic effects, not least because the closure of an account may imply loss of access to purchases and to associated virtual content <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>.

The proposed categories do not eliminate the complexity of the ecosystem nor do they intend to reduce concrete objects to a single type. They provide comparable language to decompose hybrid arrangements into controllable dimensions and to locate, precisely, which aspects were affected by a relevant modulation. This decomposition prevents formal continuity of access from functioning as an alibi for material downgrades and allows losses and degradations to be treated as legally relevant even when they manifest themselves through gradual erosions, reconfigurations of rarity, changes in display capacity or changes in reputational criteria.

With this preliminary typology, the analysis ceases to depend on episodic descriptions and comes to operate through stable parameters to recognize recurring patterns of platform-governed enjoyment, locate asymmetries of intelligibility and agency and identify when changes exceed ordinary variations and become a problem of control. This gain is intentionally obtained within the games ecosystem, as a laboratory of intensive observation, without converting the categories above into a general taxonomy of platforms. The next stage consists of situating the electronic games sector in the Brazilian normative and institutional plane only to the extent necessary to contextualize the debate, preserving the operative function of the typology and preparing the application of the grid to the case study.

The contract makes explicit that the license of access to virtual content may be obtained not only by purchase, but also by earning, including as a result of game routines: “earn it (e.g., by completing game missions or tasks)”.The provision offers grounding to describe event passes as progression objects, since the relevant utility is not an item delivered at once, but a sequence of milestones that depends on internal validation, calibration of requirements and temporal availability of the event <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024b)</2>. <3>↩</3>

The contract reserves to the supplier a broad power of administration of game content “at any time”, including to remove and reprice, “with or without prior notice”. This declaratory axis makes it compatible to treat availability windows as variables of supply, and not as exceptions. In official tone, the distinction between categories of skins reinforces that there are regimes of return and of non-continuous access, especially in stating that “Legacy skins are relatively rare because they are not always available for purchase in the Store.” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2025h)</2>. The dogmatic consequence is that time ceases to be mere context and comes to integrate the material content of what is acquired, including in the symbolic dimension of value. <3>↩</3>

The normative and institutional framing of the electronic games sector, at this point, has a strict and delimited function. The criteria-oriented typology has already stabilized the lenses through which platform-governed enjoyment can be observed and compared. It remains to situate, on the Brazilian plane, how the sector has been recognized and on which focal points it tends to be problematized, so that the study advances on institutionally intelligible ground and so that recurring tensions do not seem idiosyncratic contingencies of an isolated case.

The objective is not to compose a legislative inventory nor to reconstruct the regulatory debate in detail. What matters is to record the minimum context in which games operated as a service come to concentrate public and legal attention, highlighting vectors that reappear when enjoyment depends on an environment of continuous operation with intense private governance. Against this background, a double movement is observed. On one side, there is an effort to institutionalize games as a relevant economic and cultural activity. On the other, there is a recurrence of concerns linked to the protection of vulnerable publics, to monetization through microtransactions and random mechanisms, to the processing of personal data and to market and advertising practices integrated into the very experience of enjoyment.

The institutionalization of the sector matters because it reinforces, documentarily, the reading that games (above all under models operated as a service) are not limited to isolated products delivered in a single event. The offer is realized as an ecosystem sustained by continuous operation, permanent updating and enforcement of internal rules that integrate the material content of supply. A sufficient landmark to record this fact is Law 14,852/2024 <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2024]b)</2>, taken here as a reference of institutional recognition of the electronic games industry as an economic and cultural activity with its own relevance. The central point, for purposes of framing, is the presupposition that the sectoral statute expresses in the sense that there is, operating in Brazil, a sector consolidated as a legitimate object of state attention and of public policy structuring, with language typical of promotion, development and organization of a production chain. This dispels any impression of exceptionality of the <3>locus</3> studied and brings it closer to other mass digital markets in which enjoyment occurs over time under variable rules.

Recognition, however, does not eliminate legal tensions, it only tends to make them more predictable. In ecosystems of continued enjoyment, expectations are constituted over time, under criteria susceptible to unilateral modulation, and relevant losses may occur without formal interruption of access, whether through gradual degradation of utility, or through <1>p. 494</1> disorganization of symbolic value incorporated into what is acquired. For this reason, institutional attention is organized around vectors of friction that stem from the structure of the ecosystem, and not from isolated episodes.

The protection of children and adolescents is one of these recurring vectors. Its centrality does not derive only from concerns about content, but from the combination of interactivity, permanence of the bond and exposure to mechanisms of acquisition and permanence incorporated into the interfaces and rules of the environment. In games operated as a service, consumption decisions tend to be fragmented over time, mediated by cycles of return, signs of urgency, promises of progression, social comparison and incentives embedded in the very design of enjoyment. The cut by minors functions, thus, as an institutional trigger to make visible asymmetries of understanding and of capacity for contestation in environments governed by architecture.

In this framework, the public policy of advisory age rating plays a useful contextual role. Without functioning as prior authorization, it acts as a guiding instrument aimed at informing age suitability and relevant descriptors, and, in reaching digital products distributed by platforms, it makes explicit an important institutional premise: the experience of enjoyment is not exhausted in audiovisual “content”, since it includes conditions of interaction and circulation that can produce relevant exposures and asymmetries, above all for children and adolescents. The interest of this fact, here, is not the detail of the instrument, but what it signals about the sector. In a significant portion of cases, the risk lies in the mode of functioning of the very environment of enjoyment.

Another predictable focal point is monetization through microtransactions. In games as a service, acquisition tends to occur continuously and in segments, inserted into the very experience of enjoyment. It is not merely a payment modality. Monetization is integrated into the architecture of the environment and influences the rhythm of use, progression, access to conveniences and the very perception of value of what is acquired. The legal conflict thus shifts from the price of an isolated product to the governance of a system of offers and incentives that renews itself over time, under variable rules and with structurally accentuated informational asymmetries.

The point of greatest sensitivity appears when monetization relies on random mechanisms for obtaining items, frequently treated in public debate as loot boxes. In these cases, the utility and value of what is acquired come to depend on internal distribution regimes, on availability criteria and on limits defined by the platform, besides being articulated with signs of scarcity, time windows and rarity regimes that make decisions more dependent on anticipation, urgency and expectation. The institutional discussion <1>p. 495</1> tends, then, to concentrate on minimum transparency of the conditions of acquisition, protection of vulnerable publics and control of practices of inducing consumption, not out of moralization of the sector, but because the supplier concentrates internal criteria on availability, rotation, rarity and, where applicable, probability, under conditions of low external reconstructibility.

In this context, Law No. 15,211/2025 <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2025]c)</2> offers sufficient normative anchoring to situate the focal point by regulating, from the standpoint of the protection of children and adolescents, the loot box functionality as a mechanism of random obtaining upon payment. The interest of the statute, here, is evidential. Certain mechanics of the ecosystem have already been identified as structurally sensitive and, for this reason, amenable to treatment by criteria. Under the IOC regime, such mechanisms condense elements such as instituted rarity, anticipation, criterial opacity and unilateral modulation, with effects that may manifest themselves as material erosion of utility and reconfiguration of value, even if access remains formally available.

There is also an institutional vector linked to the fact that games operated as a service function as informational platforms. Enjoyment is realized through an identified account, inventories, usage records, performance metrics, purchase history, interaction patterns and reputational mechanisms that depend on continuous collection and processing of data. These data are not merely administrative traces. They sustain the personalization of the experience, the offer of items, rankings, validations, fraud detection, moderation and the enforcement of internal rules. The relevant contextual consequence is the intensification of structural asymmetries of information. The supplier concentrates records and parameters decisive for reconstructing changes and governance decisions, while the consumer has only partial visibility, mediated by interfaces.

In this scenario, the Brazilian personal data protection regime operates as a normative backdrop, reinforcing the institutional sensitivity of the sector in environments of continued enjoyment, especially when children and adolescents take part. The point, here, is not to turn the framing into a compliance audit, but to record that the environment of enjoyment is also an informational environment and that, for this reason, the minimum reconstruction of what changed, to what extent it changed and with what effects on utility and value becomes a relevant component for any discussion of controllability, without requiring full technical transparency or the disclosure of business secrets.

Besides minors, monetization and data, the incidence of concerns associated with market and advertising practices integrated into the experience of enjoyment is predictable. In models operated as a service, the consumer relationship is not exhausted at the initial entry. The offer <1>p. 496</1> renews itself through events, seasons, promotions, bundles and acquisition stimuli incorporated into use, so that advertising also operates as internal communication designed through storefronts, urgency messages, recommendations and highlighting mechanisms. This integration reinforces the continuous and mass character of supply and tends to activate classic consumer protection instruments aimed at adequate information, transparency and control of abusive practices.

The Consumer Protection Code, in this frame, functions as a general grammar of protection in mass relationships marked by informational asymmetry and concentration of the power to organize the offer, without this anticipating, at this point, the specific dogmatic reconstruction of the IOC regime. What is relevant, for the minimum framing, is to recognize that ecosystems of this type coexist with repeated patterns of complaints and high-scale conflicts, in which conditions of acquisition, offer criteria and effects of internal changes to the environment become central.

Finally, intellectual property appears as a latent friction because enjoyment is mediated by protected assets and by licensing regimes that delimit admissible uses, forms of access and possibilities of circulation of what is acquired. In platform-governed ecosystems, terms of use, moderation policies, transfer limits and revocation conditions are usually formulated under a logic of intangible asset management, which can intensify asymmetries of agency and reduce alternatives for reconstituting what is acquired outside the ecosystem. The usefulness of this record, here, is merely situational: consumer conflicts in games as a service frequently cross the interface between consumer protection and control prerogatives derived from licenses and intellectual property, leaving the analysis of the consequences for the proper stage of legal reconstruction.

The minimum institutional framework outlined makes it possible to understand why the electronic games sector, especially under models operated as a service, concentrates recurring legal tensions. The recognition of the sector as a relevant economic and cultural activity coexists with predictable focal points linked to the protection of children and adolescents, to monetization through microtransactions and random mechanisms, to the processing of personal data and to market and advertising practices integrated into the environment of enjoyment. These vectors do not appear as episodic accidents, but as typical effects of ecosystems in which utility is realized over time, under private governance of the environment and through rules susceptible to unilateral modulation, with structural asymmetries of intelligibility and agency.

In the <1>Riot Games</1> ecosystem, enjoyment manifests itself as a position governed by architecture, sustained by signs, modulated by internal access criteria and subjected to unilateral recompositions capable of affecting utility, prestige and expectation. For this reason, the field makes it possible to observe, in traceable and repeatedly verifiable materials, the functioning of the central categories of the Immaterial Object of Consumption, making them operative without depending on casuistic impressions. It is in this sense that the empirical <2>locus</2> functions as a means of intelligibility by illustration, since it offers a terrain in which the already stabilized reading keys cross the case and the technical-communicational environment in which it is produced.

This mobilization corresponds to an extended case approach, in which the choice of field is guided by analytical relevance, and not by statistical representativeness. The context does not act as descriptive ornament, since it allows the passage between architectural choices, modulations of enjoyment and relevant losses to be reconstructed rigorously. Generalization, here, does not occur by impressionistic extrapolation, but by controlled transit between levels of abstraction, guided by the functional equivalence of mechanisms of governance by architecture.

The movement of consolidation and of passage to the procedure of dogmatic reconstruction shows, with special clarity, how the interactive entertainment industry, by reason of the continuous provision that characterizes it, operates as an ostensive surface of exposure of the <1>Lex Plataformae</1>. This is because, in this sector, governance by architecture manifests itself in a concentrated form and is frequently assumed explicitly in the everyday administration of what is bought, in the definition of the conditions of access to goods and in the delimitation of what actually counts as permanence of the enjoyed good.

In this sense, the logic of updates, rebalancing, reformulations of access, layers of rarity and internal sanction regimes makes visible that the value of an IOC does not reside in static utility, but in a regime of intelligibility in which the prospects of balance and equivalence depend on the environment itself to exist, an environment that the supplier administers unilaterally, exercising practical sovereignty over its conditions of functioning, in the technical as well as the symbolic and, consequently, semiotic aspect.

From this perspective, semiotic vulnerability ceases to be a merely descriptive hypothesis and is confirmed as a recurring structure for describing the dynamics of asymmetry, since the platform controls, besides the technical code, the lexicon through which differences are read, displayed and recognized, so that it administers the criteria of visibility and prestige <1>p. 498</1> that stabilize the user's desire, as well as the mechanisms of commensurability capable of converting signs into access and access into reputation.

Likewise, abusive teleology departs from any moralizing reading and proves apt to identify the gearwork by which purposive deviations incorporated into design, through architectural choices, reorient the service to enable regimes of extraction and to normalize consumer losses as a principle of functioning, even if the same changes are presented, on the justificatory plane, as contingent adjustments or as inevitable effects inherent to the digital environment.

The greatest result of the path taken so far is the abandonment of fatalistic readings regarding the regulation and governance of relationships in these environments. The most important confirmation is that, once enjoyment is recognized as a position, legal control is not exhausted in contracts, prices or nominal descriptions of goods and services, since the core of the conflict comes to reside in the preservation, degradation or reconfiguration of the conditions by which the value actually acquired is, in practice, enjoyed and used by the consumer.

Functional integrity and symbolic identity, already treated as dimensions of relevant loss in IOCs, find in the ecosystem under study repeated demonstration that recompositions that preserve only name, appearance or formal access can keep the code working without preserving what, in practice, constituted the position of enjoyment that made up the consumer's legitimate expectation. In other words, it has become unequivocal that the decisive question is not whether something “still exists” in a formal sense, but whether the practical equivalence of what is acquired remains recognizable and operative, which shifts the debate to criteria of functional value equivalence and to duties of restoration that are not satisfied with empty symbolic substitutes.

The repeated use of the ecosystem ceases to be merely illustrative and comes to operate as a stabilization of parameters of controllability, because what was observed was not a sectoral particularity, but a recurring grammar of governance, that is, the structural description of a type of power that, when transposed by functional equivalence to other domains of platform capitalism, makes it possible to treat distinct problems from common parameters of reading and control.

The transposition of these parameters, however, is not confused with free extrapolation nor with justificatory intuition. Orientation by frictions and sectoral evidence does not authorize subjectivism, because analytical discipline stems from the prior explicitation of the conceptual lenses and from the requirement of verifiable reconstruction through elements attributable to the supplier and publicly recoverable, among which are update records, declared rationales <1>p. 499</1> for change, access policies and internal sanction criteria. In this frame, methodological reflexivity does not replace objectivity. On the contrary, it reorganizes it as a commitment to criteria of evidence selection and to theoretical regulation of what counts as relevant observation, reducing confirmation biases and preventing individual experiences from being confused with proof.

In light of the study developed so far, when architecture replaces direct acquisition with paths mediated by internal currency, by collateral bundles and by probability regimes, what becomes evident is not only a new sales model, but a mode of organizing consumption in which design assumes a normative role, since it redistributes relevant information, administers expectations, produces frictions and converts loss into a naturalized component of access. When technical decisions and internal policies expand the extraterritoriality of code, conditioning permanence and participation on invasive requirements or on control mechanisms that exceed the perimeter of the contracted object, the claim to practical sovereignty over the consumer and over his material means becomes evident, which reinforces the need for open auditability as a minimum requirement so that the platform does not hide behind technical opacity and industrial secrecy, and so that governance by architecture is treated as attributable, contestable conduct subject to proportionality.

At this point, the choice of <1>locus</1> has proven productive precisely by ensuring intelligibility and allowing the conceptual operators necessary for the IOC regime to manifest themselves under methodologically controllable reading criteria. A cycle of qualification thus closes, in which the typology ceased to be merely a conceptual design and became a reading instrument capable of identifying semiotic vulnerability, abusive teleology and relevant losses in their operative form, while at the same time it stabilized the criteria by which architecture can be subjected to legal control.

With the parameters of open auditability and functional value equivalence consolidated, the next step shifts the focus to institutional protection, so that the patterns already made visible and described can be converted into liability, into duties of restoration and into criteria of control under the Consumer Protection Code, in harmony with the Brazilian constitutional and economic order, so that the <1>Lex </1> <2>Plataformae</2> ceases to operate as silent sovereignty and comes to answer before the sovereignty of Brazilian Law.

From the categories already stabilized, the organization of a preliminary typology of IOCs and their recurring modes of incidence begins, to enable comparison between arrangements of supply and the reading of relevant losses. On the plane of technique and mediation, the techno-media environment was treated as a structure of perception and conduct, while the discussion about concrete design choices brought the governance of the environment back to the plane of technical decisions incorporated into architecture. On the plane of political economy, digital ecosystems were described as arrangements of continuous capture of value and production of dependence. On the semiotic plane, the commodity was understood also as a sign, so that belonging and distinction integrate value. On the methodological and institutional plane, the requirement of controllable criteria, the operative function of concepts and the legal relevance of the normativity exercised by private powers were reaffirmed.

Without a movement of typological organization, the plurality of manifestations of the IOC tends to produce two symmetrical deviations. On one side, concrete analysis degrades into descriptive narrative, in which objects, practices and interfaces accumulate as a catalog of peculiarities without identification of relevant constants. On the other, dogmatic reconstruction loses adherence to the phenomenon by operating with overly general categories, incapable of discriminating what, in platform-governed enjoyment, alters the acquired utility, reconfigures symbolic value or shifts the consumer's position in the ecosystem.

The proposed typology, therefore, does not fulfill an external classificatory function nor does it intend to exhaust reality by names. Its usefulness is internal and operative. It stabilizes criteria of <1>p. 483</1> comparison between objects and arrangements of supply, distinguishing irrelevant variations from structures decisive for the IOC regime. This cut makes it possible to treat, consistently, differences in dependence on account and infrastructure, intensity of <2>lock-in</2>, exposure to unilateral modulation, risk of gradual degradation and identity density of the object, without dissolving what is acquired into an undifferentiated “service” nor reducing the platform to a neutral distribution channel.

Typological organization, at this point, designates an instrument oriented by criteria, and not an effort of classification by apparent similarity. The focus falls on the construction of comparable classes that express legally relevant differences between objects and arrangements of supply when enjoyment is sustained by a technical-organizational environment in continuous operation. Instead of enumerating items, parameters are stabilized to describe how the object exists in the ecosystem, which structural dependencies condition it and to what extent its utility and value are susceptible to modulation of the environment.

The typological criteria derive directly from the operators already formulated for the IOC regime. Semiotic vulnerability guides the location of structural asymmetries of intelligibility and agency produced by design and governance of the environment. Abusive teleology offers a parameter for discriminating between ordinary variations of design and exploitative purposive orientations incorporated into incentives, frictions and rules of permanence. Functional integrity and symbolic identity delimit the field of relevant losses beyond binary interruption, reaching degradations of enjoyment and disorganizations of the sign-value associated with belonging, distinction and recognition.

Open auditability establishes a requirement of a verifiable minimum of justification and traceability of changes and governance decisions, without imposing total transparency or unrestricted access to business secrets. Functional value equivalence operates as a standard of restoration, preventing formal continuity of access from being confused with material preservation of the utility and value incorporated into the object. These axes define the set of measures from which the typology differentiates objects and arrangements of supply by what actually matters to the control of the regime.

With this gain in comparability, it becomes possible to treat losses and degradations as legally relevant events even when they do not take the form of explicit cancellation, distinguishing gradual erosions of utility, changes that downgrade use value and alterations that disorganize symbolic value. The difference between an object conceived as isolated content and an object whose legal existence is a position of enjoyment sustained by variable rules is also clarified. The typology makes it possible to identify when modulation exceeds <1>p. 484</1> ordinary adjustment and becomes a problem of control, in addition to providing parameters to demand minimally traceable justifications and to assess whether the restoration offered preserves, in functional terms, the utility and value incorporated into the IOC.

The cut by electronic game platforms meets a methodological reason, and not a thematic preference. These ecosystems tend to concentrate, in high resolution, defining elements of the IOC regime by combining continued enjoyment, intense private governance and an offer oriented by an architecture of incentives. Reward and progression systems, artificial scarcity, segmented monetization, social comparison and reputation devices make particularly visible the ways in which the value of the object is produced, perceived and stabilized in the environment, while at the same time they amplify asymmetries of intelligibility and agency. The centrality of collections, appearances, achievements and signs of belonging makes explicit how changes of rules, reconfigurations of interfaces and changes of visibility and display capacity can produce relevant losses without formal interruption of access.

The subsequent development begins with the framing of the digital ecosystems in which the IOC manifests itself most clearly, highlighting common traits of models sustained by continued enjoyment and by governance of the environment. Next, preliminary categories of IOC on game platforms are organized from criteria that differentiate objects and arrangements of supply by structural dependence, exposure to unilateral modulation, risk of degradation and identity density. Then, a minimum normative and institutional framing of the electronic games sector in Brazil is presented, to the extent necessary to situate the debate. The path culminates in the preparation of the case study, in which the grid built will be applied to a specific ecosystem, making it possible to verify how the operators of the IOC regime manifest themselves concretely and which tensions emerge when enjoyment depends on variable rules, validation mechanisms and unilateral changes subject to requirements of verifiable justification and adequate functional restoration.

With this organization, the passage from the conceptual apparatus to the empirical analysis occurs without loss of precision and without shift of focus. The typology stabilizes vocabulary and transforms dimensions of the IOC regime into a lens apt to recognize patterns, differentiate irrelevant variations from materially significant changes and reconstruct, consistently, relevant losses and minimum requirements of verifiable justification and functional restoration. The expected result is an examination anchored in controllable criteria, capable of sustaining a rigorous description of the selected ecosystem and preparing the stage of dogmatic reconstruction from organized evidence.

The legal problem of continuous digital consumption requires parameters of qualification, proof and attribution that do not depend on material analogies nor are limited to the contractual text. The dogmatic task is to make consumer protection operational in an environment in which enjoyment is modulated by private architecture, rules and <1>enforcement</1>, and unilateral changes can degrade value and delivery without formally suppressing access.

In this register, the reconstruction of the immaterial object of consumption is consolidated as a concretization of the “immaterial product” provided for in Article 3, paragraph 1, of the Consumer Protection Code. The decisive point is that, in platform ecosystems, the object does not present itself as a stabilized thing, but as a bundle of functional and symbolic enjoyment that depends on regimes of access, visibility, updating and governance. For this reason, adequate protection requires recognizing two complementary dimensions. Functional integrity, linked to performance, to conditions of use and to the utility actually delivered. And symbolic integrity, linked to belonging, reputation, distinction and promises of identity mediated by signs and internal equivalences of the environment, when these elements integrate the performance as offered and perceived.

The consumerist reconstruction of the IOC also requires a brake against the nominalism that separates “product” and “service” by label, without reaching the substance of governed enjoyment. In this sense, Rizzatto Nunes<1><2>402</2></1> is mobilized to sustain a sufficiently broad reading of the concept of product in the CDC, apt to encompass border zones in continuous and mediated arrangements, without dissolving criteria. This broadening has no rhetorical function. It serves to preserve the incidence of the consumer regime when delivery is realized as a enjoyment bundle dependent on architecture, and not as an isolable material object.

Conceptual discipline and the intersubjective controllability of attributions are treated as a condition of validity of the proposed regime. Thus, Karl Larenz<1><2>403</2></1>, Tércio Sampaio Ferraz <3>p. 392</3> Jr.<4><5>404</5></4> and Humberto Ávila<6><7>405</7></6> are mobilized as methodological brakes to avoid elastic categories that explain everything and prove nothing, above all in matters relating to evidentiary difficulty and the objective confrontation of the technical opacity of platforms.

On the same axis, Claudia Lima Marques<1><2>406</2></1> settles vulnerability as a structural fact of the consumer relationship and as an orientation of protection in durable bonds; Ricardo Morishita Wada<3><4>407</4></3> prevents the illusion that volume of information restores autonomy, requiring qualified intelligibility, comparability and practical usefulness; Miguel Reale<5><6>408</6></5> offers the key of integration between facts, values and norms, making it possible to bring regularities of the technical environment back to legal categories without voluntarism; and Roberto Mangabeira Unger<7><8>409</8></7> comes in at specific points to offer a substrate of resistance to the institutional fatalism that confuses contingent arrangements with technical imperatives and to reinforce bringing governance by architecture back into the field of what proves amenable to protection by Law.

The <1>Lex Plataformae</1> is treated, here, as the contemporary form of practical normativity exercised by protocols, flows, interfaces, sanctions and private adjudication procedures that organize consumption in an environment. The consumer bond comes to be <2>p. 393</2> governed not only by clauses, but by design and by continuous execution, with structural asymmetries of contestation and proof. This shifts the problem of abusiveness beyond the textual content of the contract and requires criteria capable of attributing liability for architectural decisions that downgrade enjoyment, alter equivalences and reorganize the consumer's experience without there being a traditionally identifiable “quality defect” in a product or service.

In this sense, abusive teleology is stabilized as a controllable unlawful act of architecture. It is not an effort to prohibit changes, technical evolution or the necessary internal rebalancing of digital systems. The question is the recognition of the need to distinguish legitimate change, compatible with good faith, transparency and social function, from change that diverts the purpose of the performance and converts governance into a mechanism of extraction and unilateral recomposition of value, with relevant downgrading of the enjoyment bundle. Abusive teleology appears when technical, contractual or <1>enforcement</1> mutation reorganizes delivery so as to preserve the nominal existence of the object and, at the same time, degrade its functional or symbolic substance, exploiting the asymmetry of controllability and the consumer's dependence on the environment.

To allow institutional control and minimally intersubjective proof, two operational parameters are then fixed. First, open auditability, characterized by the requirement of traceability and intelligibility of changes relevant to enjoyment, including with regard to access rules, modulations of delivery and sanction mechanisms, so as to make contestable what is produced by opaque systems. And, right after, functional value equivalence, as a criterion to assess whether the change preserves the content delivered in terms of the promised utility and experience, preventing formal substitutions from serving to cover up substantial losses. These parameters function as comparison grids to differentiate legitimate evolution from abusive practice, without requiring technical freezing nor ignoring the dynamic nature of the object.

The dialogue with the legislative framework of intellectual property rights and with the Brazilian constitutional-economic order comes in as a structural element of the regime, since exclusivities, interfaces and access regimes act as infrastructure of power and, for this reason, must be read under limits of good faith, transparency, social function and controllability. When enjoyment depends on proprietary grammars and on unilaterally administered access conditions, exclusivity is not merely a legal title. It becomes a condition of governance, with direct impact on the content delivered and on the consumer's position in the ecosystem. Legal control, therefore, needs to reach the way this infrastructure is used to modulate value, impose frictions, degrade equivalences and administer permanence.

<1>p. 394</1> The objective, in the end, is to deliver an applicable regime: criteria to qualify the IOC, identify the relevant injury in unilateral mutations and private sanctions, structure the proof of degradation of the enjoyment bundle and attribute abusiveness in a controllable key, with merely illustrative and referenced use of examples from the empirical laboratory when indispensable to fixing intelligibility, without autonomous demonstrative pretension. This set prepares the conclusions and the guidelines of institutional protection, shifting the debate from “inevitable change” to verifiable standards of legitimacy in the governance of continuous consumption.
